claims.feature: ordinary language for hobbit viewpoint vs archaic omniscient passages
claims.claim: Hobbits' points of view are recorded in ordinary language, while other passages use an archaic diction reminiscent of ancient epic and Macpherson's Ossian and convey an omniscient point of view tied to 'epic characters' like Aragorn.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'Points of View' (ch. 4) abstract, Springer

claims.claim: Tolkien's limited point of view follows nineteenth-century novelistic practice; Kullmann traces the technique from Walpole's Castle of Otranto (1764) through Pride and Prejudice, Waverley, The Mill on the Floss, Tess, Mary Webb and Buchan's Witch Wood (p. 92).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: Emphasis is laid on subjective experience rather than facts

claims.claim: Like Scott's Waverley and Buchan's David Sempill, the hobbits act as intermediaries and, in Turner's phrase quoted by Kullmann, as representatives of the normality of the reader in a strange environment (pp. 95, 123).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.feature: mediation as the function of limited POV
claims.claim: The function of the point-of-view technique is mediation: a strange environment and chain of events is brought close to the reader through the intermediate agency of characters whose point of view is recorded; the technique goes back to historical fiction (p. 119).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: brought close to the reader through the intermediate agency

claims.claim: The narrator does not explain why an event has occurred; explanation is left to other characters such as Gandalf or Aragorn, or to the hobbits' own subjective conclusions (p. 91).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: left to other characters, such as Gandalf or Aragorn

claims.claim: Psychonarration (Lanser's term) is reserved to Frodo; what Gandalf thinks or plans is left to Frodo's and the reader's speculation (p. 105).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.claim: Gandalf speaks a lot but his thoughts and feelings are hardly ever communicated to the reader in third-person narration (p. 118).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: hardly ever communicated to the reader

claims.claim: When Aragorn's viewpoint is used we are told what he sees but learn little of his thoughts and feelings (p. 114); an omniscient passage gives way to a hobbit-limited one to lend Aragorn psychological depth via Merry's gaze (p. 102).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: we do not learn much about his thoughts and feelings

claims.claim: The narrative function of Merry and Pippin is to let the novelist take a hobbit's point of view on each spreading strand of the plot after Frodo and Sam leave the Company at the end of Book 2 (p. 99).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: a hobbit's point of view to each of the spreading strands

claims.feature: focaliser shift from Frodo to Sam
claims.claim: In the first two books Frodo observes the world; later Frodo becomes the object of Sam's gaze, with Sam the focalizer in Books 4 and 6 (pp. 108, 119).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.feature: limited POV raises tension and characterises
claims.claim: As in nineteenth-century novels, the limited point of view both characterises a person and raises tension; Frodo's viewpoint conveys what he is barely conscious of, e.g. 'finding' he has put on the Ring (p. 105).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.claim: Sections told by an omniscient narrator are comparatively few, and some (the Prologue, the accounts of Bree and Minas Tirith) resemble a different text type, eighteenth-century antiquarianism such as Percy's Reliques (p. 111).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.claim: The 'epic style' first seen with the Riders of Rohan recurs particularly at moments when a battle's outcome is imminent: Helm's Deep, the siege of Gondor, and when the Ring falls into the Cracks of Doom (p. 113).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: at moments when the outcome of a battle is imminent

claims.claim: The epic passages' short sentences, parataxis, inversion and repetition, with darkness and night motifs, are reminiscent of Macpherson's Poems of Ossian (p. 116).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: short sentences, parataxis, inversion and repetition

claims.claim: In the Rohirrim passages sentences follow one another paratactically, more complex propositions are built with participles, there are few hypotactic sentences, and the effort of the journey is conveyed by inversions (p. 115).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
